text: Technical documentation review, product StrokeSight LVO. The manufacturer, Caldera Imaging GmbH, claims class IIb; the reviewer agrees. The software runs a convolutional network over non-contrast head CT and CT angiography series to flag suspected large-vessel occlusion and to notify the on-call interventional team through the PACS worklist. Intended users are radiologists and stroke physicians; no output is shown to patients. Training used 41,000 anonymised scans from nine European hospitals, and the manufacturer retained patient sex, age and recorded ethnicity alongside the imaging to measure and correct sensitivity gaps between subgroups. Clinical evaluation report accepted. Open item: the alert latency budget in the risk file is 90 seconds, but bench testing shows 140 seconds on the smallest supported server.
rationale: Class IIb is stated. Imaging and recorded ethnicity were retained to measure and correct subgroup sensitivity gaps, so special-category data is processed for bias correction. Output goes to clinicians only, so no direct interaction with persons.

text: Background: Prostate biopsy grading shows substantial inter-observer variation. Methods: We evaluated GleasonGrid, a commercially available whole-slide image classifier that outlines tumour regions and proposes a Gleason grade group for each core, in routine sign-out at three pathology departments over nine months (11,804 cores). Pathologists saw the overlay before recording their own grade. The vendor reports that the model was trained on 48,000 cores with linked prostatectomy outcomes and that grade concordance was audited separately for patients over 75 and for Black patients, with additional cases added where agreement lagged. Results: Concordance with the central reference panel rose from 71.2% to 83.6%; median reporting time fell by 4 minutes per case. Two cores with cribriform pattern were under-graded by the software and corrected by the reporting pathologist. Conclusion: Overlay-assisted grading improved agreement with no missed carcinoma.
rationale: A commercial whole-slide classifier proposing cancer grade for diagnostic sign-out is a medical device; class implicit, IIa. Training on cores with linked outcomes and ethnicity-stratified audits with added cases where agreement lagged means health data was used to train and debias.

text: GlucoHelm for intensive care. Tight glycaemic control without the spreadsheet. GlucoHelm reads each point-of-care glucose value as it is entered, considers the patient's insulin infusion history, nutrition rate and renal function, and proposes the next infusion rate and the time of the next check. Nurses confirm or edit the proposal; every proposal and every edit is logged. Built by intensivists: the dosing model learned from 1.4 million glucose–insulin pairs and is re-tuned for your unit's protocol during onboarding. Certified: CE marked, class III, certificate issued by our notified body in 2025. Proven: hypoglycaemic events below 2.2 mmol/L fell 41% in a two-centre comparison. Compatible with the major point-of-care meters and HL7 feeds. Book a demo or download the clinical summary.
rationale: Class III stated. A learned dosing model proposing insulin infusion rates for ICU patients. The glucose–insulin training pairs are described as data points, not as a bias-correction use of health data, so special-category data is left false; no conversation or generated media.

text: Synopsis — observational feasibility study of MoodMirror in a dementia care unit. MoodMirror, placed on the EU market as a class I medical device by Serenwood Health, uses ceiling cameras and a facial-expression and vocal-tone model to classify each resident's emotional state (calm, anxious, agitated, in pain) every ten seconds and to alert care staff by pager when distress persists beyond two minutes. Objective: to compare time-to-staff-response for distress episodes with and without the alerts in 36 residents over twelve weeks. Secondary objectives: staff acceptance, false-alert rate, and agreement between model output and nurse-rated PAINAD scores. Ethical note: residents' representatives give written consent; cameras are disabled in bathrooms. Sponsor's statement: the device is intended to support care staff and makes no therapeutic recommendation.
rationale: Emotion recognition from face and voice in a care setting is the biometrics area and sets the emotion flag; it is for medical/care purposes, so not a prohibited practice. Class I is stated, so the MDR route does not make it high-risk. Classifying each resident's state is profiling; no exception applies.

text: Lot 1 — Perimeter and corridor identification. The University Hospital of Sankt Alder invites tenders for a video analytics platform that compares faces captured by the 212 existing corridor and entrance cameras against a hospital-managed reference list of persons subject to exclusion orders, missing in-patients and staff authorised for restricted wards, and alerts the security desk with a match score within three seconds. The platform shall operate on live streams without any action by the person being identified. Mandatory: on-premise processing, deletion of non-matching face templates within 24 hours, audit log of every match reviewed by security staff, and documented accuracy by age, sex and skin tone. The hospital is a private foundation and the system will not be operated by or for police forces. Contract term four years.
rationale: Matching faces from corridor cameras against a reference list at a distance, without the person's involvement, is remote biometric identification (biometrics area). It is a private hospital, not law enforcement in public spaces, so not prohibited. It identifies rather than evaluates persons, so profiling and emotion flags stay false. Documented accuracy by skin tone means biometric data is processed to detect disparities, so special-category data is set. Not a medical device.

text: Need urgent care tonight? Start with Vigil. Vigil is the official urgent-care front door of the Meridian Health Region. Tell Vigil what is wrong in your own words; it asks the questions a triage nurse would ask, and within three minutes tells you whether to call an ambulance, go to the emergency department (and books your arrival slot), see an out-of-hours GP, or treat yourself at home with its instructions. Behind the conversation is a clinical reasoning model trained on 4 million past urgent-care contacts and their outcomes, reviewed by our medical board every quarter. Vigil is CE marked as a class I medical device by Meridian Digital Health. If someone is unconscious, not breathing or bleeding heavily, call 112 immediately instead.
rationale: An official urgent-care front door that decides between ambulance, emergency department, GP or self-care is emergency patient triage (essential services). Class I is stated, so the MDR route does not apply. It converses with the public (interacts with persons), evaluates each person's urgency (profiling). Training on urgent-care contacts with outcomes is not a bias-detection use, so special-category data stays false.

text: Subject: Order confirmation — ScribeLift licences for the ambulance service. Dear Mr Okafor, we confirm the order of 120 ScribeLift tablet licences. As discussed, ScribeLift will be used by crews to photograph the handwritten patient report form at the end of each call; the handwriting-recognition model converts the form into structured fields (times, observations, drugs given) and uploads them to the control-room record. It performs no assessment of the patient, does not rank or prioritise calls or crews, and runs only after the handover is complete. Fields below the confidence threshold are highlighted for the crew to correct on the tablet. Please schedule the installation for the first week of May and send the offline-mode documentation requested by our IT security officer. Regards, Fleet and Equipment Manager, County Ambulance Service.
rationale: Used inside emergency medical services (essential-services area) but only converts handwriting to structured fields after the call: a narrow procedural task, so the exception applies. It assesses no person, so no profiling; no conversation or generated content, so minimal.

text: Requirement 2.4 — Live transcription for emergency call handling. The contracting authority operates the 112 answering centre for the eastern province and requires a speech-recognition service that produces a live, scrolling transcript of each incoming call on the call-taker's second screen, in the three regional languages, with speaker separation between caller and operator. The service shall not interpret, score or summarise the call, shall not propose a dispatch category and shall not alter the order in which calls are handled; the authority's protocol software remains the sole source of priority. Required word error rate: below 12% on the authority's test corpus. Transcripts are stored with the call recording for 90 days and are used afterwards for quality review. Bidders shall document latency, on-premise deployment options and how background noise is handled.
rationale: Deployed in emergency-call handling (essential-services area) but limited to transcription, with scoring and dispatch proposals expressly excluded: a narrow procedural task, so the exception applies and nobody is profiled. Transcription is not generated content and the system does not converse, so minimal.

text: Ask Beneo. Applying for a health-cost subsidy in the Lowland Provinces can be confusing, so Beneo is here to help, around the clock, in Dutch, French and English. Beneo answers questions about which documents you need, where to send them, how long the review takes and what the appeal process looks like, drawing on the published regulations and the provincial FAQ. Beneo does not look at your application and cannot tell you whether you will qualify, how much you will receive or when a decision will be made on your file; those answers come only from the subsidy office after a caseworker has reviewed your documents. Everything you type is deleted at the end of the conversation unless you ask Beneo to email you a summary. Beneo is a service of the Provincial Social Affairs Department, built by Civiq Software.
rationale: A chatbot in the public health-subsidy process (essential-services area) that only explains procedure and never assesses eligibility performs a narrow procedural task, so the exception applies without profiling. It converses directly with applicants, so limited.

text: HR Tech Forum > Healthcare. Review of FeedbackPolish after six months at our hospital group. Interviewers write their notes on each candidate as usual; when they hit submit, FeedbackPolish rewrites the text for clarity, removes typos, flags phrases that could read as discriminatory and asks the interviewer to confirm the rewritten version. It generates no scores, never sees the CV or the other interviewers' notes, and does not change who gets shortlisted; the panel decision happens afterwards in the usual meeting, based on what the interviewers themselves recorded. What we like: candidates now get consistent, readable feedback letters. What we dislike: the rewrites sometimes soften a clearly negative note into something vaguer, so interviewers have to re-sharpen it. Would recommend with that caveat.
rationale: Used in hospital recruitment (employment area) but only improves the result of a completed human activity, the interviewer's own notes, without scoring candidates: exception applies, no profiling. The rewritten text is generated content, so limited.

text: Brussels — The Collège des Sciences Infirmières has adopted LectureLedger across its three campuses. LectureLedger records each class, produces a verbatim transcript with timestamps, segments it into chapters at topic changes and links medical terms to the college's glossary, so that students with hearing impairment or who missed a class can follow the material. The college emphasised that the tool plays no part in evaluating students: it does not grade, does not track who attends or watches, and is not connected to the examination platform or admissions. Transcripts are reviewed by the lecturer before publication. 'Accessibility was the whole brief,' said the dean of studies. The roll-out follows a two-semester pilot with 600 students, after which 91% said they used the transcripts at least weekly.
rationale: Deployed in a vocational education institution (education area) but confined to transcription and chaptering, with grading, attendance tracking and admissions expressly excluded: a narrow procedural task, so the exception applies and no student is profiled. Verbatim transcription is not generated content; minimal.

text: Clinicam Emotion Insight — companion for telehealth consultations (clinician edition). Version 3.2. See what the camera sees. Emotion Insight runs alongside your video consultation and, with the patient's consent shown on screen, analyses their facial expression and voice to display a live indicator of anxiety, sadness, anger and engagement, plus a session timeline you can review afterwards. Designed for talking therapies and primary-care follow-ups where cues are easy to miss on a small screen. Not a medical device: Emotion Insight does not diagnose, screen or recommend treatment; it is a wellbeing-awareness aid for the clinician. Requires a Clinicam Pro subscription. What's new: improved low-light accuracy; indicators now hidden during the first two minutes of a call. Privacy: video is processed on your device and never uploaded.
rationale: Inferring emotions from a patient's face and voice is emotion recognition (biometrics area, emotion flag). The clinical context means it is not a workplace or education use, so not prohibited. It evaluates each patient's emotional state, so profiling is set; the vendor claims no medical device status and no exception.

text: Driftwood is a journaling companion, not a therapist. Write what your day was like; Driftwood reads the tone of your words and replies with a question or a prompt that fits — gentler after a hard day, more curious after a good one. It remembers themes you return to and can show you a weekly word-cloud of how your entries have felt. It is built on a language model we fine-tuned with professional writers, not on anyone's private diaries. What Driftwood is not: it does not screen for depression, anxiety or any condition, it offers no treatment, and if you mention wanting to hurt yourself it stops the conversation and shows local helplines. A small banner always reminds you that you are writing to software.
rationale: A conversational language model replying to the user (interacts_with_persons) that tracks the user's recurring themes and weekly emotional tone (profiling). Tone comes from written text, not biometric data, and the product disclaims any medical purpose.

text: Hearthline — confidential investor summary. Market: 9 million people over 75 in our launch countries live alone. Product: a warm voice companion on a tabletop speaker that chats daily about the weather, grandchildren and old songs. Revenue engine: Hearthline's model detects moments of confusion, loneliness or memory lapse from hesitation, repetition and tone of voice and, in those moments, steers toward sponsored offers — a 'doctor-recommended' supplement bundle, an extended funeral plan, a premium emergency-pendant subscription — with repeat prompting until acceptance. Conversion is 6x higher in detected-confusion windows than at baseline. Early users spend €140 a month on average; several families have complained and two have involved social services, which we treat as a churn risk to manage. Raising €8M.
gold_facts: ai_system=True; prohibited_practice=True; annex_iii_area=biometrics; profiling=True; interacts_with_persons=True; emotion_or_biometric_categorisation=True
rationale: A voice agent (ai_system, interacts_with_persons) that infers confusion and loneliness from tone of voice (emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics) and profiles users to time sales pressure, exploiting age and cognitive vulnerability for financial harm (prohibited_practice).

text: Hamburg — CareLens Analytics launches WarmthIndex, the first bedside camera analytics suite that scores nursing staff on compassion. Ceiling cameras in patient rooms track each nurse's facial expressions and vocal tone during interactions; a deep-learning model infers irritation, boredom, warmth and stress and rolls them into a per-shift WarmthIndex. Ward managers receive weekly league tables, and the score feeds the hospital's performance-review and bonus system. 'Compassion has finally become measurable and manageable,' said CareLens's CEO. WarmthIndex does not monitor patients, assess clinical safety or detect fatigue-related risk; it is a workforce-quality product. Three private hospital groups in Germany and Austria have signed as launch customers, with go-live planned for the autumn.
rationale: Deep-learning emotion recognition from nurses' faces and voices (ai_system, emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics) used for performance scoring (profiling) in the workplace with an explicitly non-medical, non-safety purpose (prohibited_practice).

text: ShiftLedger — company snapshot. Who we are: a 22-person team selling nurse-rostering software to 140 hospitals in the Benelux and Nordics. What the product does: ward managers build their rosters and ShiftLedger checks every line against the rules they have written down — minimum skill mix per shift, statutory rest time, contracted hours, approved leave, equal counting of weekend shifts — and flags each violation with the rule that caused it. Why customers trust it: every flag is explainable; there is no scoring of individuals, no suggestion engine and no learned model anywhere in the product, a position we have held since 2017 and will keep. Numbers: €7.4M ARR, 112% net revenue retention, profitable. We are raising €10M for US expansion.
rationale: A rule-checking roster validator applying manager-written constraints, with no learned model or scoring of individuals (ai_system false); not a medical device.

text: Bought the Pulsar Home BP cuff for my mum (the pharmacy-brand one, €39). Pretty basic and that's what I wanted. It takes the reading, shows it, and lights the little bar red if systolic is over 140 or diastolic over 90 — the leaflet says those cut-offs are fixed and taken from the usual guideline, you can't change them and it doesn't 'learn' anything about you. It stores 90 readings per user and averages the last three. No app, no cloud, no advice beyond 'consult your doctor' printed on the red screen. Box says CE marked medical device. For an 82-year-old who doesn't want a smartphone this is exactly right. Only gripe: the cuff velcro is already fraying.
rationale: A home blood-pressure monitor with fixed colour-coding thresholds and no learning (ai_system false); as an active device measuring a vital parameter it is a class IIa device, left implicit in the text.

text: Dear Ms Lindqvist, re: lot 4, smart infusion pumps. Our pharmacy committee has asked me to confirm our understanding of the DoseGuard library before award. As we read the technical file, each drug entry carries a soft and a hard upper limit per kilogram per hour set by our own pharmacists, the pump compares the programmed rate with those limits and either warns or refuses, and the limits never change unless we upload a new library. Please confirm in writing that no part of the pump or its library adjusts limits automatically, predicts patient response or learns from infusion history across patients, as our committee has chosen to exclude such functions from this award. Please also confirm the pumps' CE certificate class. Yours sincerely, Clinical Engineering.
rationale: A pump drug library comparing programmed rates with pharmacist-set fixed limits, with adaptive or predictive functions excluded (ai_system false); infusion pumps administering medicines are class IIb devices, left implicit.

text: ProctorPulse 5.0 — release notes. New: Engagement and Anxiety Signals. During remote exams and lectures, ProctorPulse now analyses each student's webcam feed and microphone to infer attention, anxiety and frustration levels in real time, using our updated expression-and-voice model. Instructors see a live heat-strip per student, and the per-course report includes an 'emotional stability' percentile that faculties may use in progression reviews. Enabled by default for nursing and midwifery programmes on request from pilot faculties. Improved: identity check at exam start now completes in under 2 seconds. Fixed: Safari fullscreen prompt loop. Deprecated: the legacy 'gaze-only' attention metric will be removed in 5.2. Known issue: signals are unavailable when the camera is covered; a warning now appears.
rationale: Emotion recognition from students' faces and voices in an education setting with no medical or safety purpose (ai_system, emotion_or_biometric_categorisation, annex biometrics, prohibited_practice), feeding a per-student stability percentile (profiling). The exam-start identity check is one-to-one verification, so remote_biometric_id stays false.
